prompt: Stock 1 has an expected return of 18% and a volatility of 40%, stock 2 has 7% and 20%. Their correlation is 0.25. Find the minimum-variance portfolio: weights, expected return and volatility. Report percentages with two decimals.

Stocks A (expected return 8%, volatility 15%) and B (12%, 30%) are perfectly negatively correlated (ρ = −1). (a) Which portfolio of A and B has the lowest risk? (b) What is its expected return? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
With ρ = −1: σp = |xA σA − xB σB| = 0 when xA = σB/(σA + σB) = 30/45 = 66.67%, xB = 33.33%.
E = 2/3 × 8% + 1/3 × 12% = 9.33%. This portfolio is risk-free.

prompt: (a) Compute expected return, volatility and Sharpe ratio of stock A and of the fund. Should you prefer the fund if you can borrow and lend at the risk-free rate? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Stock A: returns +24% / −4% → E = 10.00%, σ = 14.00% (two equally likely states: σ = half the spread). Sharpe = (10% − 4%)/14% = 0.4286.
Fund: returns +40% / −15% → E = 12.50%, σ = 27.50%. Sharpe = (12.5% − 4%)/27.5% = 0.3091.
No: the fund has the lower Sharpe ratio. Stock A combined with borrowing reaches the fund's expected return with less risk.

prompt: (b) What is the highest price you would be willing to pay today for the fund's payoff (EUR 140 / EUR 85)? Report the price with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Find the price P at which the fund's Sharpe ratio equals stock A's (0.4286).
Expected payoff = 0.5 × 140 + 0.5 × 85 = 112.5; half the spread = 27.5.
Sharpe = (112.5/P − 1 − 0.04)/(27.5/P) = (112.5 − 1.04P)/27.5 = 0.4286 → 1.04P = 112.5 − 11.7857 → P = 96.84.
Check by replication: buy 55/14 = 3.9286 shares of A (cost 196.43) and borrow 99.59 at 4% (repay 103.57): payoff 243.57 − 103.57 = 140 or 188.57 − 103.57 = 85, cost 96.84.

prompt: A risky portfolio P has an expected return of 11% and a volatility of 18%; the risk-free rate is 3%. (a) What are expected return and volatility if you invest 70% of your money in P and 30% risk-free? (b) You have EUR 10,000, borrow EUR 5,000 at the risk-free rate and invest everything in P. Expected return and volatility? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
E = rf + x (E_P − rf), σ = x σ_P.
(a) x = 0.7: E = 3% + 0.7 × 8% = 8.60%, σ = 0.7 × 18% = 12.60%.
(b) x = 15,000/10,000 = 1.5 (weight on the risk-free asset −0.5): E = 3% + 1.5 × 8% = 15.00%, σ = 1.5 × 18% = 27.00%.
Leverage scales the risk premium and the risk in the same proportion; the Sharpe ratio stays (11 − 3)/18 = 0.44.

prompt: A stock returned 15% over the past year. A hedge fund bought it on margin: it paid 50% with its own capital and borrowed the rest at 2%. (a) What return did the fund realize on its own capital? (b) The stock's volatility is 20%. What is the volatility of the levered position? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Own capital = 50% of the position → weight in the stock x = 2, weight in borrowing −1.
(a) R = 2 × 15% − 1 × 2% = 28.00%.
(b) σ = 2 × 20% = 40.00% (the loan is risk-free).

prompt: Your friend holds only Kering stock: expected return 12%, volatility 45%. The market portfolio has an expected return of 9% and a volatility of 18%; the risk-free rate is 3%. Assume the CAPM holds. (a) Which mix of the market and the risk-free asset has the same volatility as Kering, and what is its expected return? (b) Which mix has the same expected return as Kering, and what is its volatility? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
(a) x × 18% = 45% → x = 2.5 in the market, −1.5 in the risk-free asset (borrowing). E = 3% + 2.5 × 6% = 18.00% > 12%.
(b) 3% + x × (9% − 3%) = 12% → x = 1.5. σ = 1.5 × 18% = 27.00% < 45%.
A single stock lies below the capital market line: its idiosyncratic risk is not rewarded.

prompt: Fund X offers 9% expected return with 12% volatility, fund Y 14% with 25%. The risk-free rate is 3% and you can borrow and lend at this rate. (a) Compute both Sharpe ratios. (b) What expected return can you reach with fund X (plus borrowing) at the same volatility as fund Y? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
(a) S_X = (9 − 3)/12 = 0.50; S_Y = (14 − 3)/25 = 0.44.
(b) x × 12% = 25% → x = 2.0833. E = 3% + 2.0833 × 6% = 15.50% > 14%.
With borrowing allowed, rank risky portfolios by Sharpe ratio, not by return.

prompt: Stock A: expected return 10%, volatility 15%. Stock B: 15%, 25%. Correlation −0.3. (a) Risk and return of a portfolio with 40% in A and 60% in B? (b) How much risk must you take for an expected return of 11% (only A and B)? Report percentages with two decimals.
Explain what the tangency ("super-efficient") portfolio is and why, according to Tobin's two-fund separation, every investor holds it regardless of risk aversion.
modelAnswer: With a risk-free asset, every risky portfolio P can be combined with lending/borrowing along a straight line from rf with slope equal to P's Sharpe ratio. The best line is the one tangent to the efficient frontier; the touching point T is the risky portfolio with the highest Sharpe ratio. Since leverage makes any risk level reachable, every investor gets the best return for any risk by combining T with the risk-free asset. The choice of T is objective (same for everyone given the same estimates); risk aversion only determines the mix: cautious investors lend (x < 1), aggressive investors borrow (x > 1). The tangent line becomes the new efficient frontier.
keyPoints: T = risky portfolio with the highest Sharpe ratio
Line from rf tangent to the efficient frontier
Everyone combines T with the risk-free asset
Risk aversion only sets the mix (lend vs borrow)
